939.title: Sisters and brothers of America
939.hook: a young monk greets Chicago as family, then says his tradition accepts other paths
939.carry: accept other paths, not just tolerate them
939.howItsDone: Vivekananda's Chicago addresses are printed in his Complete Works, and Hindu and Vedanta groups read them aloud in study circles and at gatherings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramakrishna's lizard on the tree: god with form, and beyond every form. Today, one of the young men who sat in his room.

Chicago. A big hall, a platform crowded with delegates from many religions, each waiting a turn to speak. Among them is a young Hindu monk. In Ramakrishna's room he was called Narendranath. Here he's Swami Vivekananda, a long way from Bengal. When his turn finally comes, he stands up, faces the crowd, and opens not with an argument or a defense of his tradition, but with a greeting.
screen: `CHICAGO.` → `A YOUNG MONK FROM BENGAL.` → `HE OPENS WITH A GREETING.`

segments.voice: The occasion was the World's Parliament of Religions, and his short talk on the opening day is printed in his collected works as the response to the welcome. His first words were: Sisters and Brothers of America. Tradition says the hall broke into applause before he could go on. Whatever the crowd heard in it, the greeting makes strangers into family before a single idea is offered. Then come the ideas. He thanks his listeners in the name of the monks of his order and of the Hindu people. His tradition, he says, taught him not only to tolerate other paths but to accept them. He gives two texts to show what he means. First, a hymn he says he learned as a boy: as rivers rising in different places all mingle their water in the sea, so the different paths people take, crooked or straight, all lead to you, Lord. Second, the Bhagavad Gita, where Krishna says, in effect: whoever comes to me, by whatever road, I reach them. Then he names what he hopes is ending: sectarianism, bigotry and fanaticism, which, he says, have filled the earth with violence. He hopes the bell that rang that morning to open the Parliament will turn out to be their death knell. A greeting, two old texts, one hope. He didn't arrive with a new teaching. He carried in songs and verses from home, and underneath them is a teaching many Hindus grow up with: the paths to God are many, and God receives people on every one of them. Not, you're wrong but I'll put up with you. Acceptance.
screen: `SISTERS AND BROTHERS OF AMERICA.` · `NOT ONLY TOLERATE, BUT ACCEPT.` · `RIVERS INTO ONE SEA.` · `WHOEVER COMES, BY WHATEVER ROAD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone whose faith or way of life is different from yours: a classmate, a coworker, an in-law, a neighbor. Silently greet them the way he greeted Chicago, as a sister or a brother, without forcing a feeling. Then picture their road as a river, starting somewhere you've never been, still running toward the sea. Notice if any part of you wants to say only my river counts. If you pray, you can hold them in a prayer you already know.
Vivekananda. Ramakrishna's disciple, the monk who greeted a hall in Chicago as sisters and brothers before saying anything else.
Your line: accept other paths, not just tolerate them. Many rivers, one sea. See you tomorrow.

940.title: Children of immortal bliss
940.hook: an Upanishad line read out in Chicago: hear, children of immortal bliss, and the atman it points to
940.carry: every soul is holy at the root
940.howItsDone: Vivekananda's paper on Hinduism is read in Vedanta study circles, and the Upanishad's call to the children of immortal bliss is chanted and quoted in Hindu talks and gatherings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vivekananda greeted Chicago as sisters and brothers and said his tradition teaches us to accept other paths, not just tolerate them: many rivers, one sea.

Hear, children of immortal bliss. That's an old line from the Upanishads, and some days after his greeting, Vivekananda read it out to the same hall in Chicago. Not ladies and gentlemen. Not friends. Not even sisters and brothers this time. Children of immortal bliss: every person in the room, named for what he believed they already were. Today, his longer talk, the one printed as his paper on Hinduism.
screen: `HEAR, CHILDREN OF IMMORTAL BLISS.` → `READ OUT IN CHICAGO.` → `WHAT YOU ALREADY ARE.`

segments.voice: The line comes from the Shvetashvatara Upanishad, where a seer calls out to all the children of the immortal and says, in effect: I have known the great one, shining like the sun, beyond the darkness, and only by knowing that does anyone pass beyond death. Vivekananda turns that call toward his listeners. They are not, at bottom, weak or fallen creatures, he tells them. He calls them children of God, sharers of immortal bliss, and holy. The soul, in the Vedanta he describes, was never born and never dies; body and mind change, but what you are underneath does not. Hindus call that self the atman, and this is one of Hinduism's biggest teachings: at the root, every person is divine. Then a second move. Religion, he says, is not finally about accepting a doctrine or agreeing with a creed. It's about realizing: being, and becoming. In the Hindu view he lays out, the point is to see the divine directly, not just to hear about it. Images, rituals and scriptures are helps along the road, steps for different people at different places. For the Hindu, he says, a person isn't traveling from error to truth, but from truth to truth, from a lower truth to a higher one. A lower step isn't an error; it's simply where someone stands. So the paper holds two things together: a very high claim about every person in the room, and a very patient view of how people get there. Children of immortal bliss, still learning to walk.
screen: `A SEER CALLS OUT TO EVERYONE.` · `THE ATMAN: HOLY AT THE ROOT.` · `RELIGION IS REALIZING.` · `FROM TRUTH TO TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Think of the name you call yourself in your worst moments, and notice it without arguing. Then try the Upanishad's name instead, child of immortal bliss, silently on the out-breath a few times, noticing what part of you resists and what part leans in; you don't have to believe it to try it on. If you pray, you can rest in a prayer you already know.
Vivekananda. The monk who stood in Chicago and called his listeners children of immortal bliss.
Your line: every soul is holy at the root. Children of immortal bliss. Tomorrow, a frog at the bottom of a well. Nine hundred forty days.

screen: `DAY 940 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE FROG IN THE WELL.`

941.title: The frog in the well
941.hook: a frog who has never left his well meets a frog from the sea
941.carry: the sea is bigger than my well
941.howItsDone: Vivekananda's frog in the well is retold in Hindu talks, interfaith gatherings and school lessons as a picture of a narrow view, with the speaker himself counted among the frogs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Upanishad's call that Vivekananda read out in Chicago: hear, every soul is holy at the root. Every soul is holy at the root.
screen: `VIVEKANANDA.` · `EVERY SOUL IS HOLY AT THE ROOT.`

segments.voice: A frog lives at the bottom of a well. He was born there, and he's done well for himself: he's fat, he's healthy, and he keeps the water clean of worms and bugs. One day another frog falls in. This one comes from the sea. The well frog is curious, and a little suspicious. Where are you from? The sea. And how big is the sea? Vivekananda told this story in Chicago, a few days into the Parliament, after speakers had been disagreeing.
screen: `A FROG IN A WELL.` → `A FROG FROM THE SEA FALLS IN.` → `HOW BIG IS THE SEA?`

segments.voice: In his short talk called Why We Disagree, he lets the story play out. Is the sea as big as my well? the frog asks, and he leaps from one side of the well to the other. Bigger, says the sea frog. A bigger leap. This big? Much bigger. You can't compare the sea with your well. So the well frog decides the visitor must be lying. Nothing can be bigger than my well, he says. Throw him out. Here's the turn. Vivekananda doesn't point the story at any one group in the hall. He puts himself in it first: he's a Hindu, he says, sitting in his own little well and thinking the whole world is that well. Then he names the others the same way. Each of us is sitting in a little well and taking it for the world. He even thanks his American hosts for trying to break down the walls of those little worlds. That's the gentleness in it. The joke isn't on the frog for living in a well. Everyone has to live somewhere, and this frog keeps his water clean. The trouble starts only at one sentence: nothing can be bigger than my well. Underneath the joke is a Hindu teaching: the truth is bigger than any one view of it. An old Rig Veda line, much quoted by Hindus, says it plainly: truth is one; the wise call it by many names. So humility about your own well isn't weakness in a Hindu; it's taking the sea seriously. Not that anyone leaves home, but that no one throws out the visitor who says the water goes farther than they've seen.
screen: `THE FROG LEAPS ACROSS HIS WELL.` · `THROW HIM OUT, HE'S LYING.` · `"I'M SITTING IN MY OWN WELL."` · `TRUTH IS ONE; MANY NAMES.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind your own well: the neighborhood, the family, the group or the way of seeing you grew up inside, and notice what's good about it, the water you keep clean. Then remember one time someone told you the world was bigger than that, and you didn't want to hear it. No judging; just breathe there, and notice the frog's leap, measuring the sea against the walls.
Vivekananda. The monk who told the Chicago Parliament he was a frog in his own well, too.
Your line: the sea is bigger than my well. Even mine, he said. Tomorrow, a teacher who said: not compassion, but service. Day nine hundred forty-one, done.

942.title: Not compassion, but service
942.hook: Ramakrishna stops mid-sentence: not compassion, but service, to every being as God
942.carry: seva: serve each person as God
942.howItsDone: Hindu temples and service groups, including the Ramakrishna Mission, describe their kitchens, clinics and relief work as seva, service offered as worship, and Vivekananda's Karma Yoga is read in Vedanta study circles alongside the Bhagavad Gita.

segments.voice: Dakshineswar, the temple garden by the river where Ramakrishna lived. One day, in the telling of Saradananda, one of his monks, the talk turns to an old devotional teaching: show compassion to all creatures. Ramakrishna slips into a deep mood and repeats the word. Compassion. Then he stops himself. Compassion? Who are you, so small, to show compassion? No. Not compassion. Service, to every being, as God.
screen: `DAKSHINESWAR.` → `COMPASSION? WHO ARE YOU TO PITY?` → `NOT COMPASSION. SERVICE, AS TO GOD.`

segments.voice: Young Narendra was in the room. He came out of the room and told the others he'd heard something wonderful, and that if he ever got the chance, he'd tell the world. Years later, as Swami Vivekananda, he did. Karma Yoga is a set of his talks on work, and a chapter called We Help Ourselves, Not the World starts by letting the air out of the helper. The world isn't waiting for any one of us to rescue it, he says. It will go on, with or without our help. So helping isn't a favor we do the world. It's a chance we're given. He calls the world a great moral gymnasium, where we exercise to grow strong. Don't stand over someone and say, here, poor fellow, take this. Be thankful they let you give. The blessing is to the giver. Then his teacher's words come back: serve the person in front of you as you would worship God, because, as Ramakrishna saw it, God is truly present in them. Hindus call this seva: service offered as worship. It's why the order he founded, the Ramakrishna Mission, runs schools, hospitals and relief work, under a motto that means, roughly: for your own freedom, and for the good of the world. Both at once. So a Hindu at a food table isn't the rescuer. She's at worship. And the person taking the plate isn't a project. They're the one she bows to, and the one who let her grow.
screen: `NARENDRA HEARD IT.` · `A GREAT MORAL GYMNASIUM.` · `THE GIVER SAYS THANK YOU.` · `SEVA: SERVICE AS WORSHIP.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you've helped lately, a coworker, a parent, a stranger, a child, and notice if any part of you is still waiting for their thanks or keeping a small score. No need to scold that part. Just turn it around, the way Ramakrishna did: see the one you helped as someone God is present in, and silently thank them for letting you serve. If you pray, you can hold them in a prayer you already know.
Karma Yoga. The yoga of work, and Vivekananda's book of talks on it, where service is worship and the giver is the one who says thank you.
Your line: seva, serve each person as God. The giver says thank you. Tomorrow, a fly finds a pot of honey. That's day nine hundred forty-two.

943.title: The fly in the honey
943.hook: a fly lands on a pot of honey to sip, and finds its feet stuck
943.carry: do the work, offer the fruit
943.howItsDone: Hindus who follow the Bhagavad Gita's teaching on work describe offering their work to God without clinging to its results, and Vedanta study circles read Vivekananda's Karma Yoga alongside the Gita.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramakrishna's word for Karma Yoga: not compassion, but service. Seva, serving each person as God, where the giver says thank you.
screen: `KARMA YOGA.` · `SEVA: SERVE EACH PERSON AS GOD.`

segments.voice: A fly finds a pot of honey. What luck. It lands on the rim, walks down to the sweet part, and starts to drink. A minute later it tries to lift off, and can't. Its feet are stuck in the very thing it came to enjoy. Vivekananda uses a picture like this in his talks on Karma Yoga, and it isn't really about flies. It's about a new job, a relationship, a project, a phone.
screen: `A FLY FINDS HONEY.` → `IT COMES TO SIP.` → `ITS FEET ARE STUCK.`

segments.voice: His diagnosis comes in a run of short reversals. We came to enjoy, and we're being enjoyed. We came to rule, and we're being ruled. We came to work, and we're being worked. The honey isn't the problem. Work isn't the problem either; again and again he tells people to work. The trouble is the sticking: work done for what it will get us, so that the getting owns us. So how do you drink without getting stuck? Not by staying away from the honey. Running from the world doesn't free anyone. The answer he calls non-attachment, and he offers two roads to it, for two kinds of people. If you believe in God, there's the road of the Bhagavad Gita, where Krishna tells Arjuna: your right is to the work, never to its fruits. Hindus call it nishkama karma, action without craving. Work, and give the results away to God, the way you'd lay a flower at a shrine. The work is yours to do. What comes of it isn't yours to clutch. And if you don't believe in God, he doesn't send you away. He offers the road of reflection and will: keep telling yourself, this outcome is not me, this praise is not me, this failure is not me, until it's true. The fly can still drink. It just learns to keep its feet on the rim.
screen: `WE CAME TO WORK; WE'RE BEING WORKED.` · `DON'T RUN FROM THE HONEY.` · `THE GITA: THE WORK, NOT THE FRUITS.` · `OR: THIS IS NOT ME.`

segments.voice: Name one thing you're working on that you care about a lot, and notice where your feet are stuck: a result you need, someone's approval, a number. If you pray, picture setting that result down at a shrine and leaving it there; if you don't, say silently on each out-breath, this result is not me. Either way, keep caring about the work, and just lift one foot off the honey.
Karma Yoga. The yoga of work: doing the work and offering the fruit, drinking the honey without getting stuck in it.
Your line: do the work, offer the fruit. Keep your feet on the rim. Tomorrow, a king, a fawn, and the small things we do every day. Day nine hundred forty-three.

944.title: Bharata and the fawn
944.hook: King Bharata, whose name India still carries, rescues a fawn, and it slowly fills his mind
944.carry: samskaras: what you dwell on, you become
944.howItsDone: Hindus tell the story of Bharata and the deer as a warning about what the mind dwells on, and many keep small daily practices, a morning puja, an evening lamp, a repeated name, because daily acts shape the self.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fly in the honey, and the Gita's answer: do the work, offer the fruit.
screen: `KARMA YOGA.` · `DO THE WORK, OFFER THE FRUIT.`

segments.voice: A king named Bharata, the king the Bhagavata says gave India its old name, Bharata-varsha, hands his kingdom to his sons and goes to live as a hermit by a river, praying all day. One morning a pregnant doe comes down to drink. A lion roars nearby. She leaps in terror, her fawn is born in mid-leap and falls into the current, and soon after, alone and terrified, she dies. Bharata wades in and carries the tiny orphan home. It's a kind thing to do. This story, from the Bhagavata Purana, is about where kindness quietly leads.
screen: `A KING BECOMES A HERMIT.` → `A FAWN FALLS INTO THE RIVER.` → `HE CARRIES IT HOME.`

segments.voice: He feeds the fawn. He worries when it wanders off. He watches for it during his prayers, and his prayers get shorter, a little each day. But the days pile up, and the Bhagavata names it plainly: attachment. The fawn slowly takes the place God held in his mind. When Bharata's life ends, the Bhagavata says, his last thought is of the deer, and he is born as a deer, one that remembers who it was. The Gita gives the rule behind it: whatever a person has dwelt on, always, is what fills the mind at the end. The ending isn't won in the last minute. It's built, day by day. Vivekananda makes the same point about character in the first chapter of Karma Yoga. Don't judge a person by their great moments, he says; big occasions can lift almost anyone. Watch the most common things. Every action and every thought leaves a mark on the mind, like a wave on a lake that sinks back down but leaves the water changed. Hindu thought calls these marks samskaras, impressions. Character, he says, is the sum of them. Bharata wasn't wicked. Loving a fawn is kind. The point is what you dwell on, you become. That's why so much of Hindu practice is daily and small: the morning puja, the lamp at dusk, the name said over and over. And it's why the horn in the parking lot and the tone of an email matter more than the speech you give once.
screen: `HIS PRAYERS GET SHORTER.` · `HIS LAST THOUGHT IS THE DEER.` · `EVERY ACT LEAVES A SAMSKARA.` · `CHARACTER IS THE PILE OF THEM.`

segments.voice: Replay one ordinary moment from yesterday, a meal, a commute, a line at a counter: how did you speak, what did your hands do, was there a flash of impatience or a small kindness? Don't judge it; just notice what impression it may have left. Then choose one small thing you could do every day this week with care, the way families light the same lamp each evening, and if you pray, offer it in a prayer you already know.
Karma Yoga. The yoga of work, and of the common daily actions where Vivekananda says character is really built.
Your line: samskaras, what you dwell on, you become. Like Bharata's days with the fawn. Tomorrow, a busy king who stayed still. See you then.

945.title: Janaka, the busy king
945.hook: a sage's son is sent to learn stillness from a king with a kingdom to run
945.carry: karma yoga: busy hands, a still self
945.howItsDone: Hindus hold up King Janaka as the model of a householder who lived the spiritual life in the middle of work, and Vivekananda's Karma Yoga is read in Vedanta study circles alongside the Bhagavad Gita.

segments.voice: Yesterday, King Bharata and the fawn: samskaras, what you dwell on, you become.

Where would you go to learn stillness? A cave, a forest, a hermit's hut. In the Mahabharata, the sage Vyasa has a son, Shuka, who already seems made for the forest. But when it's time to finish Shuka's learning, his father sends him somewhere else: to a palace, to King Janaka of Mithila, a man with a whole kingdom to run.
screen: `WHERE DO YOU LEARN STILLNESS?` → `NOT A CAVE.` → `A KING WITH A KINGDOM TO RUN.`

segments.voice: In the Mahabharata's telling, Shuka walks to Mithila and is kept waiting at the gate, and sits there unbothered. Then he's led inside, into gardens full of music and attendants and every comfort, and sits there just as still. Only then does the king come out to teach him. The stillness Shuka found in the forest, Janaka keeps in a palace, between petitions and taxes. The Mahabharata gives Janaka a saying Hindus still repeat: if Mithila burns, nothing of mine burns. Not that he wouldn't fight the fire; a king would. But who he is doesn't burn with it. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna points to him by name: by action alone, Janaka and others reached perfection. That's the ideal of karma yoga, and Vivekananda drew it in his own picture: the ideal person finds intense activity in the deepest silence, and in the middle of intense activity finds the silence and solitude of the desert. Such a person, he says, walks the busy streets of a big city as calm as if in a cave. That's the Hindu householder's path: you don't have to leave the family, the job or the city to walk toward God. Serving each person as God, offering the fruit of the work, choosing what you dwell on, this whole week has been one skill: stay in the middle of the world without being swept off by it. So the student, the parent with three jobs, the nurse on a double shift, each has Janaka's kingdom, and Janaka's still place. Which leaves a question: how do you actually find that quiet? Karma Yoga mostly answers with work. Vivekananda has another book that goes straight at the mind, and that's tomorrow.
screen: `SHUKA WAITS, UNBOTHERED.` · `IF MITHILA BURNS, NOTHING OF MINE BURNS.` · `BY ACTION ALONE, JANAKA.` · `A DESERT IN THE BUSY STREET.`

segments.voice: For the first part of the sit, let the world in: every sound, every itch, every thought about what's next, without pushing any of it away. Then, changing nothing outside, look for the still place underneath, the part of you noticing the noise that isn't noisy itself, and rest there while the sounds go on. If you pray, you can hold that stillness in a prayer you already know.
Karma Yoga. The yoga of work, Janaka's way: busy hands, and a still self in the middle of the busiest street.
Your line: karma yoga, busy hands, a still self. Janaka's way, and a whole week in one picture. Day nine hundred forty-five, done.
